The United States abandoned the gold standard in March and April 1933, when the government passed a series of laws and executive orders to suspend the gold standard for United States currency [5]. This action required anyone holding significant amounts of gold coinage to exchange it for US dollars at the fixed price, after which the US would no longer pay gold on demand for the dollar, and gold would no longer be considered valid legal tender for debts [5].

This event marked the end of Roman rule in Britain [1]. Some historians, like Michael Jones in "The End of Roman Britain" (1998), suggest that the Britons took charge of their own affairs after Rome did not provide the requested assistance [2]. The Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire led to the downfall of the Incan empire, primarily due to the introduction of diseases to which the native population had no immunity [2]. Additionally, the Incan population faced significant declines, with some regions suffering a population decline ratio of 58:1 during the years 1520-1571 [2]. The Spanish conquest also involved the systematic destruction of Incan cultural practices, such as their sophisticated farming system known as the vertical archipelago model of agriculture [1].

The Spanish imposed a labor system called mita, which forced Incan families to work in gold and silver mines, particularly the large silver mine at Potosí [1]. Furthermore, the last Incan resistance was suppressed when the Spaniards annihilated the Neo-Inca State in Vilcabamba in 1572 [3]. Forced labor and socioeconomic changes under Spanish rule contributed to the collapse of the Incan economy and society [3].

While the Spanish conquest was a key factor, some scholars argue that the Inca Empire may have been in decline prior to the arrival of the Spanish [5]. For instance, Emperor Huayna Capac ruled the Inca Empire in 1528, and scholars like Jared Diamond suggest that the empire may have been weakening [5].

Tornadoes most commonly occur in the United States, particularly east of the Rocky Mountains [1]. The Great Plains, the Midwest, and the Mississippi Valley are all areas prone to tornadoes [1]. The states hit most frequently include Oklahoma, Kansas, and those in "Tornado Alley" [1][3]. Texas experiences the highest number of tornadoes of any U.S. state [4]. Florida, despite having the most tornadoes per unit area, mostly experiences weak tornadoes [1][3]. Strong tornadoes, however, are more common in states like Oklahoma and Kansas [1][3]. While tornadoes can occur in every U.S. state, including Alaska and Hawaii [2], they are relatively rare in the western states west of the Rockies [1].
